llm.paragraph: Without having reviewed the specific underlying studies, a generic expectation based on general familiarity with this research area would be that antioxidant supplementation with vitamin C and/or E most often shows no significant effect on exercise training adaptations, though results likely vary by context. A model would anticipate that blunting effects, when observed, tend to be reported more with high-dose combined vitamin C and E supplementation, particularly in the context of endurance training and molecular markers of mitochondrial biogenesis or antioxidant enzyme upregulation, reflecting interference with redox-sensitive signaling pathways. Conversely, no-effect findings might be expected under conditions of lower doses, shorter intervention durations, resistance training paradigms, or when outcomes are measured as performance or strength rather than cellular signaling. Enhanced adaptation would be the least expected outcome, plausibly limited to populations with baseline nutrient deficiency or high oxidative stress burden. Given that the aggregate summary indicates a majority "no effect" direction with only moderate agreement (~70%) across a small number of grounded papers (5 papers, 11 findings), this expectation aligns loosely with what a model might predict, but confidence should be regarded as low given the limited and mixed evidence base, and this description should not be taken as a substantiated synthesis of actual literature.
